standard.constat: Short circuit: phase and neutral meet without passing through a load.
standard.cause: A direct path connects phase to neutral around {composant}.

apprentissage.explication: Your circuit has a short circuit: the current found a shortcut connecting the phase straight to the neutral, without crossing any load (lamp, motor…). With no load to hold it back, the current becomes enormous in a fraction of a second.
apprentissage.cause: Somewhere around {composant}, a wire connects phase to neutral with nothing in between.
apprentissage.indice_1: Follow the wire leaving the phase: does it meet a load before reaching the neutral?
apprentissage.indice_2: Check the wires connected to {composant}, terminal {borne}: one of them creates the shortcut.
apprentissage.correction: Remove the direct link between phase and neutral, and always route the current through a load.

standard.constat: Short circuit: two different phases are connected together.
standard.cause: Two phases meet at {composant}, with no load between them.

apprentissage.explication: Two different phases are connected together: this is the most violent short circuit, because the voltage between two phases is even higher than between phase and neutral. In real life, this causes a dangerous electric arc.
apprentissage.cause: A direct path connects two phases around {composant}.
apprentissage.indice_1: Check your phase order: do two wires coming from different phases end up connected at the same point?
apprentissage.indice_2: On the power terminals of {composant}, make sure each phase stays on its own line.
apprentissage.correction: Separate the two phases: each phase must feed its own path and never touch another directly.

standard.constat: Short circuit: two opposite potentials meet without a load.
standard.cause: A load-free shortcut exists around {composant}.

apprentissage.explication: The current found a shortcut with no load on its way. With no resistance to limit it, it rises brutally: that is a short circuit.
apprentissage.cause: A direct, load-free path exists in the area of {composant}.
apprentissage.indice_1: Look at the blinking area: follow each wire and ask yourself whether it goes through a load.
apprentissage.indice_2: Disconnect the suspicious wires around {composant} one by one and simulate again: the fault will disappear once the shortcut is gone.
apprentissage.correction: Remove the direct path and route the current through a load.

standard.constat: The circuit is open: {composants} cannot be powered.
standard.cause: The electrical loop is not closed all the way to this load.

apprentissage.explication: Current only flows in a closed loop: it must leave the source, cross the load, and come back. Here, the loop to {composants} is broken somewhere — the current cannot complete the trip.
apprentissage.cause: A connection is missing, or a contact is open, on the path leading to {composants}.
apprentissage.indice_1: Start from the source and follow the path with your finger up to the load: where does it stop?
apprentissage.indice_2: Also check the switches and contacts along the way: an open contact breaks the loop even if every wire is in place.
apprentissage.correction: Complete the loop: every terminal on the path must be connected, and the required contacts closed.

standard.constat: {composant} has burned out: it is out of service.
standard.cause: It suffered stress beyond its rating (short circuit, excessive voltage or current).

apprentissage.explication: {composant} received more than it can handle and is destroyed. In real life this means smoke, a burning smell, and a component to replace — exactly what protective devices exist to prevent.
apprentissage.cause: An excessive stress (short circuit, overvoltage or overcurrent) went through {composant} without a protection stopping it in time.
apprentissage.indice_1: Check the journal: which fault happened right before the burnout? That is the culprit.
apprentissage.indice_2: Ask yourself which protection should have saved {composant}: is it present, properly rated, properly placed upstream?
apprentissage.correction: Fix the original fault, replace {composant}, and make sure a suitable protection sits upstream.

standard.constat: Breaker {composant} tripped: everything downstream is de-energized.
standard.cause: It detected a fault on its circuit and cut the power to protect it.

apprentissage.explication: Breaker {composant} did its job: it detected a problem and cut the power to protect the circuit and the people. Everything connected after it is now de-energized.
apprentissage.cause: A fault (usually a short circuit) occurred downstream of {composant}.
apprentissage.indice_1: Do not reset it right away: first find WHY it tripped. What happened downstream?
apprentissage.indice_2: Check the journal: the fault that caused the trip is recorded right before it.
apprentissage.correction: Find and fix the downstream fault, then reset {composant}.

standard.constat: {composant} tripped on overload: the current stayed above its {calibre} rating for too long.
standard.cause: Too much power drawn downstream compared to the breaker rating.

apprentissage.explication: The current exceeded what {composant} (rating {calibre}) accepts, for too long. Its thermal protection — a bimetal strip heated by the current — eventually cut the power. This is the overload protection: deliberately slow, to tolerate brief peaks but stop lasting excess.
apprentissage.cause: The loads downstream draw more current than the rating of {composant} allows ({courant_max} A continuous).
apprentissage.indice_1: Add up what your downstream loads consume: is it compatible with a {calibre} rating?
apprentissage.indice_2: Two options: reduce the load, or review the rating — but careful, a bigger rating must still match the wire size it protects.
apprentissage.correction: Reduce the downstream load or adapt the rating within what the conductors allow, then reset.

standard.constat: {composant} tripped instantly: the current exceeded its magnetic threshold.
standard.cause: A very high, sudden current (typical of a short circuit) went through the {calibre}, curve {courbe} breaker.

apprentissage.explication: {composant} cut the power in a split second: that is its magnetic trip unit, the protection against short circuits. Unlike the thermal unit (slow, for overloads), the magnetic unit reacts instantly when the current explodes. Its curve {courbe} sets the reaction threshold.
apprentissage.cause: A sudden current, far above the curve {courbe} threshold of the {calibre} rating, went through {composant} — almost always a downstream short circuit.
apprentissage.indice_1: An instant trip almost always means a short circuit: look for where phase and neutral (or two phases) meet downstream.
apprentissage.indice_2: If the circuit is healthy but a motor is starting, its inrush current can exceed a B curve: that is exactly what C and D curves are for.
apprentissage.correction: Remove the downstream short circuit (or match the curve to the load type), then reset.

standard.constat: The residual current device {composant} tripped: part of the current is leaking to earth downstream.
standard.cause: The current going out through the phase does not fully come back through the neutral — the difference flows to earth (likely insulation fault).

apprentissage.explication: The toroid of {composant} constantly compares the outgoing current (phase) with the returning current (neutral). Normally they are identical. Here part of the current escapes to earth — often through the chassis of an appliance with faulty insulation — and as soon as that leakage reaches the IΔn sensitivity, the RCD cuts the power. This is the protection of PEOPLE against indirect contact.
apprentissage.cause: A downstream insulation fault makes current leak to earth through the protective conductor (PE).
apprentissage.indice_1: Do not keep resetting: the RCD will trip again as long as the leakage exists. Find WHICH downstream appliance leaks to earth.
apprentissage.indice_2: Unplug the loads one by one and reset each time: the one that makes it trip again carries the insulation fault (measure it with an ohmmeter between a terminal and the chassis).
apprentissage.correction: Identify the appliance with the insulation fault, repair or replace it, then reset {composant}.

standard.constat: {composant} is not designed for this voltage: network at {reseau_u}, rated voltage {ue}.
standard.cause: The breaker's rated voltage (Ue) does not match the network voltage.

apprentissage.explication: Every breaker is designed for a specific voltage, its rated voltage Ue. {composant} is rated {ue}, but your network is at {reseau_u}. Under-rated, it can be destroyed; over-rated, it may not break the current properly. In real life, you always read Ue on the front face before installing.
apprentissage.cause: The rated voltage of {composant} ({ue}) does not match the network voltage ({reseau_u}).
apprentissage.indice_1: Compare the voltage written on the component with your source voltage: same family (230 V? 400 V?)?
apprentissage.indice_2: Ask yourself whether your circuit is phase-to-neutral (230 V) or phase-to-phase (400 V): the equipment choice depends on it.
apprentissage.correction: Replace {composant} with a model whose rated voltage matches the network.

standard.constat: The short-circuit current ({icc}) exceeds the breaking capacity of {composant} ({icn}).
standard.cause: The breaker cannot interrupt such a high fault current: it may be destroyed without breaking it.

apprentissage.explication: Very dangerous situation: the short-circuit current ({icc}) is higher than what {composant} can interrupt (its breaking capacity Icn: {icn}). In real life, the breaker can explode or weld its contacts WITHOUT cutting the current — the protection itself becomes the hazard.
apprentissage.cause: The breaking capacity Icn of {composant} is lower than the prospective short-circuit current at this point of the installation.
apprentissage.indice_1: The breaking capacity (Icn, in amps or kA) is written on the breaker face: compare it with the calculated fault current.
apprentissage.indice_2: The closer to the source, the higher the fault current: equipment near the supply needs a higher Icn.
apprentissage.correction: Choose a breaker whose Icn exceeds the prospective short-circuit current at this point.

standard.constat: The circuit never settles: something switches on and off in a loop.
standard.cause: A component cuts its own supply, which re-triggers it, endlessly.

apprentissage.explication: Your circuit oscillates: something activates, which cuts its own supply, which deactivates it, which powers it again… forever. The circuit never finds a stable state. In real life, you would hear a component chattering non-stop.
apprentissage.cause: A feedback loop exists: a component controls (directly or not) its own supply through a contact that opens when it activates.
apprentissage.indice_1: Find the chattering component: what powers it, and what does it cut when it activates?
apprentissage.indice_2: Check your NO and NC contacts: an NC used where an NO belongs (or the opposite) often creates this loop.
apprentissage.correction: Break the loop: the component must not cut its own supply (review the contact type or the holding circuit).

standard.constat: The circuit contains no power source.
standard.cause: Without a source, no current can flow.

apprentissage.explication: Every circuit needs an energy source: it creates the potential difference that sets electrons in motion. Without a source, your assembly is just scenery — nothing can flow.
apprentissage.cause: No source (network, power supply) is placed or connected in this circuit.
apprentissage.indice_1: Which component provides the energy in your assembly? Find it in the catalog.
apprentissage.indice_2: Once the source is placed, locate its terminals: all your wiring will start from them.
apprentissage.correction: Add a power source and connect your circuit to its terminals.

standard.constat: The circuit contains no load (receiver).
standard.cause: Without a load there is nothing to power — and closing the loop would short the source on itself.

apprentissage.explication: A circuit exists to power something: a lamp, a motor, a coil… that is the load. Without one, not only does your circuit do nothing, but closing the loop would create a short circuit: nothing would hold the current back.
apprentissage.cause: No receiver is present in this circuit.
apprentissage.indice_1: What do you want to operate? Add that receiver: it gives the current a purpose (and a resistance).
apprentissage.indice_2: Place the load on the current path: the current must cross it to go from phase to neutral.
apprentissage.correction: Add a load and route the current through it.

standard.constat: Thermal relay {composant} tripped: its safety contact (95-96) opened.
standard.cause: The motor drew more than the relay setting ({courant_max} A) for too long — a sign of mechanical or electrical overload.

apprentissage.explication: Thermal relay {composant} protects the MOTOR (not the wires: that is the breaker's job). The motor drew too much current for too long — as if it were straining — and the relay opened its 95-96 contact, cutting the contactor coil: the motor stops before it burns.
apprentissage.cause: The absorbed current stayed above the setting of {composant} ({courant_max} A): motor straining, jammed, or setting too low.
apprentissage.indice_1: Follow the chain: relay tripped → contact 95-96 open → contactor coil de-energized → motor stopped. Find these links in your diagram.
apprentissage.indice_2: Compare the relay setting with the motor's rated current: the setting must match the motor plate, neither too low (nuisance trips) nor too high (no protection).
apprentissage.correction: Fix the cause (motor overload or wrong setting), then reset the relay.

expert.resume: {composant}: differential trip — one pole carries no current while the others conduct.

standard.constat: Thermal relay {composant} tripped on PHASE LOSS: one of its poles saw no current while the others were conducting.
standard.cause: One phase of the motor circuit is broken (wire unplugged, loose terminal, blown fuse) — or, on single-phase, the phase is not looped through all three relay poles.

apprentissage.explication: A three-phase motor needs all THREE phases, like a stool needs its three legs. If one phase disappears, the motor keeps turning on two phases but strains: the two remaining windings overheat. Relay {composant} detects this by comparing its bimetal strips: the one on the dead phase stays cold while the others heat up — this imbalance trips faster than a classic overload.
apprentissage.cause: One power pole of {composant} carries no current at all: phase broken upstream or downstream (unplugged wire, open contact, fuse), while the other poles still conduct.
apprentissage.indice_1: Compare the relay's three poles: which one sees no current? Trace that pole's wire back to the source, then down to the motor, to find the break.
apprentissage.indice_2: Trade tip: on a SINGLE-PHASE circuit, loop the phase through all three relay poles (in series), otherwise the relay believes a phase is lost — which is exactly what just happened.
apprentissage.correction: Restore the missing phase (reconnect the wire, tighten the terminal), or loop the phase through all three poles on single-phase, then reset the relay.

standard.constat: {composant} receives the phase, but the current has no return path.
standard.cause: The link to the neutral is missing or broken (terminal {borne} involved).

apprentissage.explication: Current is like a runner on a track: it must complete the full loop. Here, the phase does reach {composant}, but there is no return path to the neutral — the current is at the start line with no road back. Careful: the wire is still live, so it is dangerous in real life, even though nothing lights up.
apprentissage.cause: Terminal {borne} of {composant} is not connected to the neutral (link missing or broken).
apprentissage.indice_1: Your current leaves the phase — but how does it come back? Follow the path after {composant}.
apprentissage.indice_2: Look at terminal {borne} of {composant}: is it connected to anything that leads to the neutral?
apprentissage.correction: Connect the output of {composant} to the neutral to close the loop.

standard.constat: {composant} is connected to the neutral, but no phase feeds it.
standard.cause: The phase-side link is missing or broken (terminal {borne} involved).

apprentissage.explication: {composant} has its return path (the neutral), but nothing brings it energy: no phase reaches it. It is a return road with no departure — the current has no starting point to flow.
apprentissage.cause: Terminal {borne} of {composant} is not connected to any phase (link missing, or an open contact cuts the supply).
apprentissage.indice_1: The return is there — but where is the supply? Where should the phase of {composant} come from?
apprentissage.indice_2: Follow the path from the source: is there a switch or an open contact blocking the phase before {composant}?
apprentissage.correction: Bring the phase to terminal {borne} of {composant} (and close the required contacts along the way).

expert.resume: {composant}: ON, but L/N not powered — no 24 V.

standard.constat: {composant} is on, but the AC input (L and N) is not powered.
standard.cause: Without phase and neutral at the top, the 24 V DC output stays at zero.

apprentissage.explication: A switch-mode power supply turns mains (230 V~ on L and N) into 24 V DC. If you do not bring the mains to the top terminals, the converter has nothing to transform: the + and − outputs at the bottom stay dead. This is not a short circuit — the PSU simply has no AC feed.
apprentissage.cause: Terminals L and N of {composant} are not connected to an active mains source (phase + neutral).
apprentissage.indice_1: Look at the top of {composant}: is there a phase wire (L) and a neutral wire (N) from the mains?
apprentissage.indice_2: Also check that the mains source is active (simulation started) and that any upstream breaker is closed.
apprentissage.correction: Wire L and N of {composant} to the mains (phase and neutral), start the simulation, then use + and − at the bottom for your 24 V control circuit.

standard.constat: The coil of {composant} is rated {bobine}, but A1–A2 see {reseau}.
standard.cause: The voltage or the kind (AC / DC) at the coil terminals does not match the nameplate.

apprentissage.explication: A contactor coil only accepts the voltage printed on its nameplate. {composant} is rated {bobine}. Here A1 and A2 receive {reseau}. Overvoltage (e.g. 230 V on a 24 V coil): overheating, smoke, possible destruction — the contactor will not stay pulled in. Undervoltage (e.g. 230 V on a 400 V coil): not enough force, no pull-in. Wrong AC/DC: matching volts is not enough.
apprentissage.cause: A1–A2 of {composant} are not fed as the nameplate says ({bobine}).
apprentissage.indice_1: Read the voltage engraved on the coil (24 V DC, 230 V AC…). Compare it with what you actually wired on A1 and A2.
apprentissage.indice_2: A 24 V DC control circuit comes from the + and − of a power supply, not from the phase and neutral of the 230 V mains.
apprentissage.correction: Feed A1–A2 with the nameplate voltage, or replace {composant} with a coil suited to {reseau}.

standard.constat: {composant} is rated {plaque}, it receives {recu}.
standard.cause: The voltage or the kind (AC / DC) does not match the nameplate.

apprentissage.explication: A lamp, a pilot light or a motor only works at the voltage printed on its nameplate. {composant} is rated {plaque}. Here it receives {recu}. A 230 V AC lamp on 24 V DC stays dark: the number of volts is not enough, and DC is not AC. Two identical lamps in series still see the source voltage and stay on.
apprentissage.cause: {composant} is not fed as its nameplate says ({plaque}).
apprentissage.indice_1: Read the voltage engraved on {composant}. Compare it with the source you actually wired.
apprentissage.indice_2: 24 V DC comes from the + and − terminals of a power supply. A 230 V AC lamp belongs on phase and neutral.
apprentissage.correction: Replace {composant} with one rated {recu}, or feed it with {plaque}.

standard.constat: Short circuit: two opposite potentials meet without a load.
standard.cause: A load-free shortcut exists around {composant}.

apprentissage.explication: The current found a shortcut with no load on its way. With no resistance to limit it, it rises brutally: that is a short circuit.
apprentissage.cause: A direct, load-free path exists in the area of {composant}.
apprentissage.indice_1: Look at the blinking area: follow each wire and ask yourself whether it goes through a load.
apprentissage.indice_2: Disconnect the suspicious wires around {composant} one by one and simulate again: the fault will disappear once the shortcut is gone.
apprentissage.correction: Remove the direct path and route the current through a load.
